Every evening after Mats fell asleep, Sofia opened a small green notebook at the kitchen table in their Copenhagen flat. She wrote the date and only facts.
14 May: M said I never asked him to fetch Mum from the station. I asked at breakfast and texted at 11.
16 May: M said I screamed. I said "please stop" twice, not loud.
The notebook lived in her work bag, not at home.
On Saturdays she walked along the harbour with her old friend Ulla. Today she read out three entries and asked, "Am I being unfair?"
Ulla listened to all of it. "No. This matches what you've told me each week, and what I saw at your birthday." She squeezed Sofia's arm. "Would you talk to someone at the counselling centre too? I'll look up the number with you."
Sofia nodded. For the first time in months, her memory felt like solid ground.

qa.q: Where did Sofia keep the notebook?
qa.a: The notebook lived in her work bag, not at home.

qa.q: How did Sofia feel after Ulla's reply?
qa.a: She felt steadier and relieved; for the first time in months, her memory felt like solid ground.

qa.q: Which of Sofia's choices protected her sense of reality?
qa.a: Writing only dated facts in private, checking them with Ulla, and agreeing to contact the counselling centre gave her anchors outside Mats's version of events.

qa.q: How does Ulla see the notebook entries?
qa.a: Ulla sees them as matching what Sofia has said each week and what she saw herself, so she trusts Sofia's account and offers practical help.

grounding: A young woman keeps a private dated record of events and checks it with a trusted friend and a counsellor, anchoring her perception outside the person casting doubt.

passage:
The counselling room at the logistics company had one window and a box of tissues nobody touched. Imran slid a printed page across the table.
"It's a log," he said. "Since March, my manager, Mr Kapoor, keeps saying I never got his instructions, or that I imagine the deadlines he moved. So after every call I email him a summary: As discussed, delivery report by Friday. Then I note the date here."
Yamini, the staff counsellor, read it slowly. "How has it felt, keeping this?"
"Honestly? Like proof I'm not losing my mind. Last week he said I'd agreed to Sunday work. I opened the email thread in front of him. He changed the subject."
"Your records are clear, and your worry makes sense," Yamini said. "Shall we look at what the formal complaint route would need, so you have options?"
Imran let out a long breath and nodded.

qa.q: What does Imran email after every call?
qa.a: He emails Mr Kapoor a summary of what was discussed, such as "delivery report by Friday".

qa.q: What does keeping the log mean to Imran?
qa.a: Keeping the log makes Imran feel reassured, like proof he is not losing his mind when Mr Kapoor denies things.

qa.q: How does Yamini support Imran at this point?
qa.a: Yamini listens, confirms the records are clear and the worry makes sense, and offers to look at the complaint route so Imran has options rather than only doubts.

qa.q: How might Mr Kapoor react now that his instructions are on record?
qa.a: He can no longer easily deny what was agreed; changing the subject when the email was shown suggests the record leaves little room to rewrite events.

grounding: A young man keeps dated email summaries of his manager's instructions and checks his perception with a counsellor, protecting his sense of what happened.

passage:
Subject: can I check something with you?

Dear Kavitha,
This might sound strange. For months, my manager has been telling me I never said things I'm sure I said. "You didn't flag that delay." "You never asked for leave." I started believing I was losing my mind.
So, on my counsellor's advice, I began keeping a private notebook. Date, time, what I said, who else was there. I also started sending short emails after every conversation: "Just confirming what we discussed…"
Last week he said I'd never mentioned the budget problem. I opened my sent folder. There it was, on the 4th, with his reply: "Noted."
I'm writing because you were in that meeting on the 4th. Do you remember me raising it? I don't need you to take sides. I just need one person outside my own head to tell me what they saw.
Thank you for being my anchor.
Lavanya

qa.q: On what date did Lavanya's email about the budget problem go out?
qa.a: On the 4th.

qa.q: How had Lavanya been feeling before keeping the notebook?
qa.a: Lavanya felt confused and frightened, starting to believe the problem was Lavanya's own mind.

qa.q: What steps did Lavanya take to protect her sense of reality?
qa.a: She kept a private dated notebook, sent confirming emails after conversations, followed her counsellor's advice, and asked Kavitha what she saw.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel reading this email?
qa.a: Kavitha may feel concerned for Lavanya and glad to be trusted as an outside check.

grounding: An adult keeps a private written record, works with a counsellor, and checks perception with a colleague outside the situation.

passage:
Thanks for having me on the show, Noor. I'm Hafsa, and I want to talk about the notebook.
Two years ago, I was living with someone who kept telling me things didn't happen. "I never said that." "You're remembering it wrong." After a while, I didn't trust my own head.
A friend gave me a small green notebook. She said, "Just write down what happens. Date and facts. Nobody reads it but you."
So I did. "14th March, he said he'd pay the rent. 20th March, he said he never said that." At first it felt silly. After three months, I read it back, and I cried. It wasn't my memory. It was a pattern.
I took the notebook to a counsellor. She read a few pages and said, "Your memory is fine." That sentence gave me my ground back.
If you're listening and you feel confused all the time, get a notebook. And tell one person outside.

qa.q: What colour was Hafsa's notebook?
qa.a: It was a small green notebook.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when she read the notebook back after three months?
qa.a: Hafsa felt overwhelmed and relieved, crying on seeing that the problem was a pattern, not memory.

qa.q: What steps helped Hafsa trust her own mind again?
qa.a: Keeping dated facts in a private notebook and taking it to a counsellor, who confirmed her memory was fine.

qa.q: How might listeners who feel confused all the time respond to Hafsa's story?
qa.a: They might feel less alone and more willing to write things down and tell someone outside.

grounding: A young adult describes protecting a sense of reality by keeping a dated record and checking it with a friend and counsellor outside the situation.

passage:
I'm Suraj, Shalini's younger brother. I only saw pieces of what was happening, but I saw enough.
Last winter, Shalini started saying "maybe I imagined it" a lot. Her boyfriend would promise something, then deny he ever had. She'd end up apologising. She looked tired all the time.
Then, in February, I noticed she carried a small diary everywhere. Once, at our kitchen table, she showed me a page. "12 Feb: he said he'd come to Papa's birthday. 13 Feb: he said I made it up." She asked me, "Were you there when he said it?" I was. I told her so.
She nodded slowly, like something had clicked into place. She started seeing a counsellor after that. She'd come back from sessions quiet, but steadier.
I don't know everything she felt. But I know that diary, and people outside, helped her trust her own mind again.

qa.q: What did Shalini's diary say for 12 Feb?
qa.a: "12 Feb: he said he'd come to Papa's birthday."

qa.q: How did Shalini seem to feel when Suraj confirmed he was there?
qa.a: Shalini seemed relieved and steadier, nodding slowly as if something clicked into place.

qa.q: What helped Shalini protect her sense of reality?
qa.a: Keeping a dated diary, checking with Suraj who was there, and starting to see a counsellor.

qa.q: How does Suraj see his role in what happened?
qa.a: Suraj sees himself as one outside anchor, not knowing everything Shalini felt but glad to confirm what he saw.

grounding: A brother observes his sister keeping a dated diary and checking events with him and a counsellor, anchoring her reality outside the doubt.

passage:
Monday: For the third time, Vijay told the team that Ishita had "invented" a deadline he had set. Ishita went pink and apologised, then sat in the washroom wondering if her memory was going.
Thursday: That evening she opened a private notebook at home and wrote: date, what was said, who was there. She added the old ones too: 3 March, deadline given in standup, Neel present. She called her friend Soumya and read it out. "You're not making this up," Soumya said. "You have dates."
Three weeks later, Tuesday: Vijay tried again. "I never asked for the draft by today." Ishita kept her voice level. "You asked in Friday's standup, and your email that afternoon says so." She forwarded it. Vijay went quiet. That evening she booked a session with the company counsellor, to plan what to do if it kept happening.

qa.q: Who was present when the deadline was given on 3 March?
qa.a: Neel was present at the standup.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel after the first incident?
qa.a: Ishita felt embarrassed and shaken, going pink and wondering in the washroom whether her memory was going.

qa.q: Which of Ishita's steps protected her own perception?
qa.a: Writing dates and witnesses privately, checking the notes with Soumya, and keeping the email gave her anchors outside Vijay's version.

qa.q: What would change if Ishita had kept everything to herself?
qa.a: Without notes, the email or a friend's check, Ishita might have kept apologising and doubting her memory, and Vijay's account would have gone unchallenged.

grounding: Shows a person keeping a private record of dates and events, checking it with a trusted friend and a counsellor, so reality rests on anchors other than the doubter.
